title: In the beginning, Being
hookLine: the father goes back to the beginning: there was only Being, one, without a second
carry: one being, without a second, became many
last: THE CLAY — MANY NAMES, ONE CLAY.

cards: But what was there before? Before Grandma, before the dinosaurs, before the world? Kids ask it at bedtime.
Philosophers ask it for a living. The Upanishads ask it too. Uddalaka has told his son that under every pot there's clay.
Now Shvetaketu needs to know what the clay of everything is. So the father goes back to the beginning, with a creation story short enough for bedtime.

teach.h: BEING ALONE, ONE WITHOUT A SECOND.
teach.b: Uddalaka begins: sad eva somyedam agra asit, ekam evadvitiyam. In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. Sat: Being, what is.
Then he takes on a rival view head-on. Some say that in the beginning there was non-being, and Being came out of it.

teach.h: HOW COULD BEING COME FROM NOTHING?
teach.b: But how could something come from nothing? No, my dear. In the beginning there was Being.
Then the turn that gives today's line.

teach.h: IT THOUGHT: LET ME BE MANY.
teach.b: That Being thought: let me be many. Let me grow forth. It sends out heat.
The heat, in turn, thinks: let me be many, and sends out water. That's why, Uddalaka says, when a person is hot or grieving, they sweat or weep: water comes out of heat.
The water thinks the same thought, and sends out food. That's why, wherever it rains, there's plenty to eat.
Heat, water, food: the three basic stuffs everything else will be made of. And notice the motive.
The text names nothing outside Being that makes it act. It simply thinks, let me be many. Later Hindu thinkers read that line in more than one way.
Some hear the one truly becoming the many. Others hear the one appearing as many while staying one. But either way, here is where the clay leads.
For a Hindu reading Uddalaka, nothing you meet stands outside that one Being: not the stars, not the food, not the people at your own table.

how: Uddalaka's opening line, 'Being alone, one without a second', is quoted again and again in Hindu philosophy, and Vedanta teachers use ekam evadvitiyam as a short summary of their teaching.

o: a seat for meditation, from the word for sitting
the empty nothing the world came out of
Being, what is: what was there in the beginning

games.q: Uddalaka's creation story — tap the pairs.

s: Uddalaka says the world came from nothing
he rejects that view: how could Being come from non-being?
Being thought: let me be many
and became heat, then water, then food.
the order is water, then heat, then food
heat first, then water, then food.

games.q: you're Shvetaketu. your father says the world began as Being alone. you ask: then what made Being act? what does the text say?
o: a god outside it pushed it into motion.
nothing outside it: it thought, let me be many.
heat came first and stirred it up.
games.why: the text names nothing outside Being. it simply thinks, let me be many, and sends out heat, then water, then food.

practice: Let the room fade, the sounds, the light, the chair, and let your thoughts thin out until there's little left but the plain fact of being here.
Rest there, and when something arises on its own, a sound, a thought, a sensation, watch the one becoming many, and let it come and go.

wordCard.voice: Sat, Being, what is, the real. Uddalaka's creation story: Being alone, one without a second, which thought, let me be many, and became heat, water and food.

orig.note: Sanskrit sat: being, what is, the real. Uddalaka's word for what was there in the beginning.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: one Being, without a second, became many. Heat first, then water, then food. That's day three hundred forty-one.

sources.q: sad eva somyedam agra asit, ekam evadvitiyam

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.2.2–4 (non-being rejected; let me be many; heat, water, food)
